description: We are interested in the intersection of computer science and biology.
summary:
Space radiation is an invisible hazard. Measuring exposure is essential—but understanding its biological effects is the next challenge.
AEROL connects radiation exposure with the question that matters: how is the astronaut’s body responding? Our interactive dashboard combines public NASA ISS radiation data, white blood cell trends, and TERRA—an RNA molecule involved in maintaining chromosome ends and responding to DNA damage—to explore patterns across a mission.
Our prototype lets astronauts investigate radiation timelines and simulated exposure scenarios alongside biological observations. AEROL Buddy, our plant-inspired wearable companion, adds daily well-being check-ins and optional self-care actions inspired by NASA’s research on space gardening and isolation.We explore whether TERRA patterns could help inform individualized monitoring, while recognizing that TERRA is not yet a validated marker of radiation injury.
Our vision is a connected wristband and app that links radiation alerts with biological follow-up with a builtin AI tool that helps flag unexpected changes for medical review. AEROL moves beyond displaying radiation exposure toward a framework for understanding biological response and supporting personalized astronaut health monitoring.
details:
When radiation exposure changes, astronauts need more than a number, they need context and a next step. AEROL connects radiation monitoring, general health trends and biological follow-up, helping astronauts and ground teams understand what is changing and coordinate a response.

Our prototype combines wearable health signals,  including heart rate and skin temperature, with radiation measurements, TERRA observations and white blood cell trends. An astronaut-facing watch simulator presents alerts, trends and follow-up actions, while an Earth-based dashboard supports medical and research review. The proposed physical system connects wearable sensors, dosimetry and externally collected laboratory results.

The demonstration follows a practical sequence: exposure changes, the watch alerts the astronaut, a structured health check begins, and information reaches Earth for review. A shared simulation clock and simulated communication delays show how onboard awareness and ground support can remain coordinated when immediate communication is unavailable.

Using NASA RadLab ISS radiation measurements and published biological observations, AEROL explores the connection between environmental exposure and biological response. TERRA is an RNA molecule involved in maintaining chromosome ends and responding to DNA damage. Our research hypothesis is that radiation exposure may be associated with increased TERRA and changes in white blood cell profiles. Bringing these signals together creates a framework for investigating responses across a mission.

Our simulation framework compares low Earth orbit with hypothetical deep-space missions. Users can explore cumulative radiation exposure and experimental TERRA and blood-count scenarios across different mission durations and exposure conditions. Historical measurements, projected radiation and hypothetical biological responses are labeled, preserving the distinction between observations and scenario assumptions.

An integrated large language model brings health, radiation and biological information together to explain trends and support experimental mission-response projections. Our longer-term goal is to learn from previous missions to improve future simulations, incorporating destination, trajectory, shielding and solar activity. These exploratory outputs support research and medical review rather than autonomous diagnosis.

AEROL Buddy adds a personal dimension to the wearable experience. This plant-inspired companion offers daily check-ins on mood, energy, sleep and crew connection, followed by optional actions such as a breathing pause, a crew conversation or a quiet reset. Inspired by NASA’s space-gardening and isolation research, Buddy complements biological monitoring with everyday self-care.

We built the prototype using a Python backend, SQLite storage, an integrated LLM, and HTML, CSS and JavaScript interfaces for desktop and phone browsers. Its modular design supports additional sensors, datasets and prediction models. Throughout development, we considered communication delays, limited biological sampling, data provenance and the need to make complex information understandable.

AEROL’s innovation is connecting exposure, physiology, biological research and self-care in one coordinated workflow. Our vision is for every mission to help protect the next, turning today’s exposure and biological data into tomorrow’s personalized monitoring, so astronauts can travel farther with a clearer understanding of their health and stronger support throughout the journey.
